messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: State-space modeling with multiple observations
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: State-space modeling with multiple observations
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Haakon here. I ran your code and looked at the variables.

str(dat.try, 1)
shows that your linear predictor is of length 274.

but
length(unique(dat.try$i))
= 252
length(unique(dat.try$space.1))
= 2

And so, the latent model ("below the linear predictor"), for i

f(i, model="ar1", replicate=space.1, fixed=FALSE)

has 252*2 = 504 different marginals that you are estimating.
(This f() wants 2 identically distributed replicates of 252 variables)

As I read you, you only wanted 24, from 2 sites in 12 years.
Then, make sure that
length(unique(dat.try$i)) = 12

Does that help?

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

From:  <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Richard Feldman <rich...@eco.umass.edu>
Date:  Tuesday 31 May 2016 17:16
To:  R-inla discussion group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com>
Subject:  [r-inla] Re: State-space modeling with multiple observations

Thank you, Bob. I had seen "replicate" before but didn't investigate it further. In fact, the Ross et al. 2012 PLoS One paper uses that notation [i.e., f(space, replicate=time), f(time, replicate=space)] but because they do not show the observation model, I was unsure how to use replicate in a state-space context.

I tried implementing f(z, model="ar1') on a subset of my data. It runs but I'm not sure it's giving the proper results. The model returns random effects of "i" and "j" (the indices of x_t and x_(t-1)) equal in length to the total data (n.plots*n.sites*n.years) whereas I was expecting the estimates at the site level n.sites*n.years. I imagine I am coding the indices incorrectly.

In my test case, I have 2 sites and 12 years. In site 1, I have 10 plots and in site 2, I have 11 plots. Therefore, I am expecting 24 random effects estimates. However, after running the model, I am getting 504 estimates for "i" and "j" (21 plots*12 years*2 transects). The year and spatial autocorrelation random effects seem correct; the former has a length of 22 (n.sites*(n.years-1)) and the latter a length of 48 (n.sites*n.years).

I will describe my data and model but I am also attaching R and RData files.

py<-n.plots*n.years #21 plots x 12 years
sy<-n.sites*n.years #2 sites x 12 years

#Data
Y <- matrix(NA, py+sy-n.sites, 2)
Y[1:(n.py, 1] <- data$Count #Counts for every year in every plot, followed by NAs
Y[1:(sy-n.sites) + (py), 2] <- 0 #NAs at the plot level and 0's at the site level

So, here my data matrix is "uneven," with the first part consisting of plot level data (n.plots*n.years = 21*12 = 252) and the second part consisting of the site level data (because the 0's of the latent variable are at the site level; n.sites*n.years = 2*12 = 24 - the last year of data at each of the two sites = 22)

#Indices
id1  <- (1:sy)[-((1:n.sites)*n.years)] #last year removed from each site
id2  <- (1:sy)[-c(1,((1:(n.sites-1))*n.years)+1)] #first year removed from each site

i  <- c(1:py, id2) # indices for x_t;
j  <- c(rep(NA,py), id1)     # indices for x_{t-1};
w1 <- c(rep(1,py), rep(-1,(sy-n.sites)))  # weights for j

Here, I wasn't sure if I should have two different "site" index variables. One concatenates: a replication of sites for each of the corresponding plots and years (e.g. site #1 replicated 120 times for each of its 10 plots and 12 years) and a replication of sites for each year (e.g replicated 12 times). The second site index concatenates: a replication of NA for each plot and year followed by the replication for year.

i.site.1<-c(as.numeric(factor(data$Site)), rep(as.numeric(factor(unique(data$Site))), each=n.years)[id2])
i.site.2<-c(rep(NA, py), rep(as.numeric(factor(unique(data$Site))), each=n.years)[id2])
i.years<-c(rep(NA,py), rep(as.numeric(factor(unique(data$Year))), times=n.sites)[id2])
i.covariate<-c(rep(NA,py),covariate$Total[-((1:n.sites)*n.years)])

dat.try=list(Y=Y, i=i, j=j, w1=w1, cov=i.covariate,
             space.1=i.site.1, space.2=i.site.2, time=i.years)

formula <- Y ~ f(i, model="ar1", replicate=space.1, fixed=FALSE) + f(j, w1, copy="i") +
  f(space.2, model="bym", graph=adj.s, replicate=time) + f(time, cov, model="iid", replicate=space.2)

After running the model, the estimates of "i" and "j" have a length of 504. Can anyone point out my mistake?

Thank you!!

On Friday, May 27, 2016 at 10:42:28 AM UTC-5, Richard Feldman wrote:
>
> Dear INLA community,
>
>
> I am hoping to use INLA for a state-space model of population dynamics. After some reading, I understand how to use augmented matrices, estimating separate likelihoods on two columns. However, in my case, I have multiple observations of an animal’s abundance (counts) per site (i.e. multiple plots per site). I would like to use the plot level information to estimate a site level mean:
>
>
> y_(i,j,k)~rpois(μ_(j,k) ), where plot i is nested in site j for year k
>
>
> In my data, I have 941 total plots divided among 99 sites (hence there is an uneven number of plots per site; it ranges from 6 to 24) for 52 years. I have a covariate measured annually at the site level as well as an adjacency matrix for the sites. My goal is to test whether the effect of the covariate on counts varies from year-to-year.
>
>
> If I ignored the grouping of plots into sites and measured everything at the plot level, my data would look like (and here I am indebted to Ruiz-Cardenas et al. 2010 and Ross et al. 2015):
>
>
>
> nd <- n.plots*n.years
>
> Y <- matrix(NA, nd*2-n.plots, 2) #second half of data will not contain the final year
>
> Y[1:nd, 1] <- my.data$Count #counts in first column followed by NAs
>
> Y[1:(nd-n.plots) + nd, 2] <- 0 #NAs in second column followed by 0
>
>
>
> id1  <- (1:nd)[-((1:n.plots)*n.years)] #density dependence will have the last year removed
>
> id2  <- (1:nd)[-c(1,((1:(n.plots-1))*n.years)+1)] #w_t will have the first year removed
>
> ix1  <- c(1:nd, id2)  ## all years for observation model, missing first year for process model
>
> ix1b <- c(rep(NA,nd), id1) ## indices for density dependence
>
> wx1b <- c(rep(1,nd), rep(-1,nd-n.plots)) ## weights for density dependence
>
> iw22 <- c(rep(NA,nd),id2) ## indices for w_t
>
>
>
> i.plots<-c(rep(NA,nd),as.numeric(factor(my.data$plot))[-((1:n.plots)*n.years)]) #plot level spatial autocorrelation
>
> i.years<-c(rep(NA,nd), as.numeric(factor(my.data$year))[-((1:n.plots)*n.years)])
>
> i.covariate<-c(rep(NA,nd), Covariate$Value[-((1:n.plots)*n.years)]) #plot level measure of covariate
>
>
>
> dat.try=list(Y=Y, ix1=ix1,ix1b=ix1b,wx1b=wx1b,iw22=iw22,covariate=i.covariate, space=i.plots, time=i.years, )
>
>
>
> formula <- Y ~ f(iw22,model="iid") +   f(ix1, model="iid",initial=-10, fixed=TRUE) + f(ix1b,wx1b, copy="ix1",fixed=FALSE) + f(space, model="bym", graph=adj.plots) + f(time, covariate, model="iid")
>
>
>
> m.1 <- inla(formula, data = dat.try, family = c("poisson","gaussian"),
>
>                control.family = list(list(link="log"),
>
>                                      list(initial=10, fixed=TRUE)),
>
>                control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
>
>                control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))
>
>
>
> However, I am not clear whether it is possible to implement the model such that the observation and process models have different lengths (941 observations in the observation model and 99 in the process model) and how does the program “know” how to group the plots into the appropriate site.
>
>
>
> I have seen a similar method applied in Ross et al. 2012 PLoS One where they have an observation model: y_(i,j,t)~NegBinom(μ_(j,t),∅), and a process model: z_(j,t)~log⁡(μ_(j,t) )~β_(0,j)+β_(1,j,t)+ε_(j,t)+n_(j,t) but unfortunately the code they provided doesn’t show the indices for the data matrix.
>
>
> Thank you very much for any help or hints.

--

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: State-space modeling with multiple observations
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: State-space modeling with multiple observations
messages.body_plain:
If I understand you correctly, yes, you want to choose the same "i" for all 11 (and later 10) plots in the same transect.

However, how you write it now, you are saying the last year of the first transect (i=12) is connected to the first year of the second transect (i=13). I do not think this is what you want.

Rather: I think you want replicate. With the same grouping (1 for everything in the first transect, 2 for everything in the second transect). I believe that i= c(rep(1:12, each=11), rep(1:12, each=10)) and then append NA's as you have indices belonging to the other observation likelihood.

Do you agree?

# Also
If you want to have the SAME effect, not just a shared mean, you can drop the replicate

# Copy?
I do not understand why you have j as a copy of i. This makes me a bit hesitant about my answers.

# Index across obs likelihoods
In the model you sent me, there was "i" indices across both "observation likelihoods". This is strange to me, do you want the same effect? I would probably use a separate replication index for this other likelihood. Same index (when both in i and the replicator index) means you get the exact same random variable (with same posterior mean estimate and marginal).

# To be on the safe side
If you want to, you can write down the entire model. E.g.
y^{(1)} \sim ...
y^{(2)} \sim ...
\eta^{(1)} = ... + ... + ...
etc.

And send me this (in latex or handwritten). Together with a version of the code you believe in. And I can check whether the two are the same.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

Hello Haakon et al.,

Yes, I see now about using replicate f(i, model="iid",...,replicate=space.1), where space.1=c(rep(1, 12*11), rep(2, 12*10)).

Using "copy" and indices "i" across both likelihoods comes from the state-space literature, specifically Ruiz-Cardenes, Krainski, and Rue. 2012. Computational Statistics and Data Analysis 56:1808-1828.

Stealing directly from their code available on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>

set.seed(123456)

W = 0.5
V = 1.0
n = 100
x0 = 0.00
w  = rnorm(n,0,sqrt(W))
v  = rnorm(n,0,sqrt(V))
x  = y = rep(0,n)
x[1] = x0   + w[1]
y[1] = x[1] + v[1]
for (t in 2:n){
  x[t] = x[t-1] + w[t]
  y[t] = x[t]   + v[t]
}

m = n-1

# building the augmented model
# ----------------------------
Y <- matrix(NA, n+m, 2)
Y[1:n,     1] <- y              # actual observations
Y[1:m + n, 2] <- 0              # faked observations

# indices for the INLA library
# ----------------------------
i  <- c(1:n, 2:n)              # indices for x_t
j  <- c(rep(NA,n), 2:n -1)     # indices for x_{t-1}
w1 <- c(rep(NA,n), rep(-1,m))  # weights for j
l  <- c(rep(NA,n), 1:m)        # indices for w_t

# formulating the model
# ---------------------
formula <- Y ~ f(i, model="iid", initial=-10, fixed=T) +

               f(j, w1, copy="i") +

               f(l, model ="iid") -1

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Thank you for the reply. I would love to hear more about why or if I do not need the fake zeroes. I’ll try the best I can to describe my aims mathematically, though, I have very little experience and training doing so (which, is a part of the problem...). So apologies if the notation just makes things more confusing.

y_(i,j,t)~rpois(μ_(j,t) ) #observation model

z_(j,t)~log(μ_(j,t) )~β_0(j)+β_1(j)*z_(j,t-1)+ε_(j,t)+n_(j,t) #process model

ε_(j,t) ~ N(π_(j,t), σ2) #second level of the hierarchical model

π_(j,t) ~ α_1 + α_2(t) *covariate_(j,t) + ω_(j, t) #second level process model

n_(j,t) has a spatially autocorrelated error structure

The key points are:

- Plot level observations (y_(i,j,t)) from the same site are drawn from a poisson distribution with the same mean

- The site level mean (and, thus, the observations) are related to the previous year’s mean (i.e. density dependence)

- The estimate I’m most interested in solving is α_2, which dictates the effect of the covariate on population size every year. In essence, I want to know year-to-year variation in the magnitude and direction of the effect of the covariate. And the effect is to be measured after controlling for the effects of density dependence and spatial autocorrelation.

messages.subject: An endless spatio-temporal modelling
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I would like to predict the spatio-temporal schistosomiasis risk in my study area using sample village-level data (i.e., No. of infected individuals and No. of population at risk) between 2005-2010. I ran the following coding, but it is always endless. Can someone point out where the problem is? Thank you!

BTW, I have changed resolution of the mesh, but the procedure is still endless.

mydata<-read.csv("G:/schistosomiasis/guichi/guichi.csv",header=TRUE,sep=",")
head(mydata)

mydata is as follows
  VillageID         CM  POINT_X POINT_Y  R6 R8 year    river
1         1 孔井居委会 543823.2 3390654 981 70 2005  1026.56
2         2 十里居委会 543072.0 3386813 669  0 2005  2212.47
3         3 长岗居委会 543256.7 3388562 638 31 2005  1474.28
4         6     低岭村 572830.9 3391545 973 15 2005 15680.83
5         7     河口村 571306.7 3390207 829  8 2005 16375.35
6         9     龙池村 565170.0 3383849 866 10 2005 20806.61
the projection coordinate information (CRS("+proj=utm +zone=50 +datum=WGS84")

guichi.mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc.domain=border, max.edge=c(5000, 10000))
plot(guichi.mesh)

#############estimate
mydata$time<-rep(1:7,each=41)
guichi.spde<-inla.spde2.matern(mesh=guichi.mesh,alpha=2)

A.est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=guichi.mesh,loc=cbind(mydata$POINT_X,mydata$POINT_Y),
group=mydata$time,n.group=7)

s.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name="spatial.field",
n.spde=guichi.spde$n.spde, n.group=7)

stack.est <- inla.stack(data=list(y=mydata$R8,n=mydata$R6),
A=list(A.est, 1), effects=list(c(s.index,list(Intercept=1)),
list(river=mydata[,8]/1000)), tag="est")

####predicted locations within border were selected
guichi.pred<- readOGR("G:/schistosomiasis/guichi","pred_all")
river.pred<-guichi.pred$NEAR_DIST

A.pred <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=guichi.mesh,
loc=coordinates(guichi.pred),
group=1, #selected day for prediction
n.group=7)

stack.pred <- inla.stack(data=list(y=NA,n=1),
A=list(A.pred,1),
effects=list(c(s.index,list(Intercept=1)),
list(river=river.pred/1000)),
tag="pred")

stack<-inla.stack(stack.est,stack.pred)

formu<- y~ -1+Intercept+river+f(spatial.field, model=guichi.spde,
group=spatial.field.group, control.group=list(model="ar1"))

output<-inla(formu, data=inla.stack.data(stack,spde=guichi.spde),
family="zeroinflated.binomial.1",Ntrials=n,
control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack),compute=T))

In the end, the interface of R is as follows but the programming was still running

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/--RLHD4yEaRc/V1UcPU-zkgI/AAAAAAAAAB0/yAGnnsWh0BMnIuO7DuoLbeeJBAuavXqBwCLcB/s1600/QQ%25E6%2588%25AA%25E5%259B%25BE20160606140608.jpg>

messages.subject: Too flexible SPDE in a spatial poisson model?
messages.subject_clean: Too flexible SPDE in a spatial poisson model?
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA group,

we are developing a predictive spatial  poission model of deer,
using a combination of spatial and other covariates. We are assuming an SPDE-type spatial effect.
Fitting the model results in a very good R2 between predicted and observed deer counts.

However, when we compare the prediction of the fixed effects only, removing the spatial effect, the R2 becomes incredibly low, on the order of 0.01 (see also the attached plot of predicted VS true deercount when including and excluding the spatial effect).  In comparison, a simple poisson regression excluding random effects gets an R2 of 0.06 - still not brilliant, but definitely better than the result of the INLA model.

My guess is that the spde is "too flexible", exactly following the observed counts with no remaining variation to fit the other covariates to. Would this be a reasonable interpretation, and if so, how would you go about fixing it? After reading previous posts on here relating to SPDE models,  I've played around with the alpha, which doesn't affect anything, and with prior.variance.nominal. Prior.variance.nominal does do something, in that when it's set to 10^-7 or so, the SPDE becomes very slowly varying; but any lower than that, and the estimated random effects become "exact" again. A model without the SPDE leads to R2's of 0.25 or so...
Another approach I've been thinking about is to make the grid coarser, thereby forcing inla to average the effect of multiple data points, but I'm not if this is sensible.

On a tangential note, I am painfully aware that using R2 for model diagnostics on a spatial predictive poisson model is terribly abusive - any suggestions for better ways of evaluating/reporting model fit and predictive performance would be much appreciated!

Best regards,
Gustaf

Code here:
----------
##Hull and mesh
prdomain2 <- inla.nonconvex.hull(coords2, convex= -0.05, resolution=c(100,100)) ## Changing convex gives more or less bendy boundary
mesh4<- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=prdomain2,
loc=points,
cutoff=10000,
offset=c(3000, 10000),
max.edge=c(15000, 100000) ) ## Change maxedge to get bigger/smaller resolution
plot(mesh4)
points2 <- cbind(rd2$E,rd2$N)
points(points2[,1], points2[,2], pch=19, cex=.5, col="red")

##Setting up the spde model

exp<- 7
deerdens.spde2 = inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh4,
alpha=2,
prior.variance.nominal = 10^(-exp),
prior.range.nominal =NULL ##priors here can/should be tweaked to adjust how bendable the random fields is.

)
A.est = inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh4, loc=coords2)

#use the inla.stack function
spde.index2 = inla.spde.make.index(name="spatial.field", n.spde=deerdens.spde2$n.spde)

#note random effcts have to be listed in covars here
data.all <- rd2
effects = list(c(list(intercept=rep(1,deerdens.spde2$n.spde)),spde.index2),
covar=data.all[,c("ALL.ROADS", "ELEVATION", "ELEV.TRI", "ASPECT", "ASPECT.TRI",
"P.GRASS", "P.MIXEDF", "annualNDVI_grass",
"avSlopeGreenUp_grass", "annualNDVI_mixedforest",
"avSlopeGreenUp_mixedforest", "DEER.COUNT.TYPE", "YEAR")])

effects.fixed = list(list(intercept=1),
covar=data.all[,c("ALL.ROADS", "ELEVATION", "ELEV.TRI", "ASPECT", "ASPECT.TRI",
"P.GRASS", "P.MIXEDF", "annualNDVI_grass",
"avSlopeGreenUp_grass", "annualNDVI_mixedforest",
"avSlopeGreenUp_mixedforest", "DEER.COUNT.TYPE", "YEAR")])

#DEER.DENSITY ~ f(DEER.COUNT.TYPE, model = "iid") + f(YEAR, model = "iid") + ALL.ROADS + ELEVATION + ELEV.TRI + ASPECT + ASPECT.TRI +
# P.GRASS + P.MIXEDF + annualNDVI_grass + avSlopeGreenUp_grass + annualNDVI_mixedforest + avSlopeGreenUp_mixedforest

stack.est2 = inla.stack(data=list(y=data.all$DEER.DENSITY),
A=list(A.est, 1),
effects=effects,
tag="est")

stack.predall = inla.stack(data=list(y=NA),
A=list(A.est, 1),
effects=effects,
tag="predall")
stack.predfixed = inla.stack(data=list(y=NA),
A=list(A.est, 1),
effects=effects.fixed,
tag="predfixed")

stack.all<-inla.stack(stack.est2,
stack.predall,
stack.predfixed)

formula4=y ~ -1 + intercept + ALL.ROADS + ELEVATION + ELEV.TRI + ASPECT + ASPECT.TRI +
P.GRASS + P.MIXEDF + annualNDVI_grass + avSlopeGreenUp_grass +
annualNDVI_mixedforest + avSlopeGreenUp_mixedforest + f(DEER.COUNT.TYPE, model = "iid") +
f(YEAR, model = "iid") + f(spatial.field, model=deerdens.spde2)

deer.density.output4 = inla(formula4,
family = "poisson",
data = inla.stack.data(stack.all),
control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack.all),compute=TRUE),
control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),
control.fixed=list(expand.factor.strategy='inla'),
control.results=list(return.marginals.random=FALSE,
return.marginals.predictor=FALSE))

predest <- inla.stack.index(stack.all, 'est')$data
predall.ndx <- inla.stack.index(stack.all, 'predall')$data
predfixed.ndx <- inla.stack.index(stack.all, 'predfixed')$data

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Too flexible SPDE in a spatial poisson model?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Too flexible SPDE in a spatial poisson model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gustaf,

If I understand you correctly, you want to penalise the complexity of the spde model. We have a new prior meant to do this, which has been successful in a couple of cases. I attach code for it here.

Note: I would not say "the spde is too flexible",I would say "we use priors for the hyper-parameters that represents too flexible models". But maybe this is what you mean.

local.inla.spde2.matern.new <http://local.inla.spde2.matern.new> = function(mesh, alpha=2, prior.pc.rho, prior.pc.sig)
{
  # Call inla.spde2.matern with range and standard deviation parametrization
  d = INLA:::inla.ifelse(inherits(mesh, "inla.mesh"), 2, 1)
  nu = alpha-d/2
  kappa0 = log(8*nu)/2
  tau0   = 0.5*(lgamma(nu)-lgamma(nu+d/2)-d/2*log(4*pi))-nu*kappa0
  spde   = inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh,
                             B.tau   = cbind(tau0,   nu,  -1),
                             B.kappa = cbind(kappa0, -1, 0))

  # Change prior information
  param = c(prior.pc.rho, prior.pc.sig)
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$prior = "pcspdega"
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$param = param
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$initial = log(prior.pc.rho[1])+1
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta2$initial = log(prior.pc.sig[1])-1

  # End and return
  return(invisible(spde))
}

# And then call the function with
sig0 = 1; rho0 = .3 #rho0 is typical range, sig0 typical sd
# - YOU MUST SET rho0 , e.g. to half the length/width of your space
# - You may reduce sig0 to have less spatial effect
# - You may increase rho0 additionally, to make the spatial effect smoother

spde = local.inla.spde2.matern.new <http://local.inla.spde2.matern.new>(mesh, prior.pc.rho = c(rho0, 0.5), prior.pc.sig = c(sig0, 0.5))

# Taking out the spde
If you have fitted the model with the spde, it is a bit difficult to "take out" the spde part and only think about the rest. This is because the (posterior) distribution of the spatial field is heavily correlated with the distributions of the fixed betas (in cases where you have spatial covariates). (I.e. feel free to do it, but be careful with interpretation)

Example: The spatial field is sometimes heavily confounded with the intercept, but for predictions, this does not matter at all, since they are integrated out jointly.

# Suggestions for evaluating the model
In sample:
- R2 with median posterior, for checing mean fit
- Check how many of the points fall inside 95% credible intervals (marginally), for checking "uncertainty fit"
- dic, waic (for checking Bayesian model fitness)

Out of sample:
- cpo (may take some time though) (for checking marginal out-of-sample fit, mean and uncertainty)
- hold-out sets (corresponding to your desired "prediction scenarios")

# code in the inla call
... control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic = TRUE) ...

# More
I tried to answer your main questions. I hope you will ask further questions, or restate the ones you are the most interested in :)

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.subject: zero-inflated models
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA experts,

I have the following model structure:

Y(i) ~Bin(Ntrial, p(i))

p(i)=p_a + (1-p_a)*prob(i)

logit(prob(i))=alpha + beta* x(i)

I would like to estimate alpha, beta and p_a

After simulating data I have tried to estimate these parameters using the zeroinflated.binomial.1 likelihood (see R code below ). However the 95%CrI do not include the original parameter estimates. Is there an alternative approach I should be using in INLA?

#####################################################################

x1=rep(1:200,20)

n=length(x1)

beta=-0.1

alpha=1.2

eta=rnorm(length(x1),x1*beta+alpha,sd=0.005)

prob=exp(eta)/(1+exp(eta))

p=0.2

pp=p+(1-p)*prob

plot(pp)

y=rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = pp)

data = list(y=y,x1=x1)

formula = y ~ 1+x1

result1 = inla(formula, family = "zeroinflatedbinomial1", data = data, Ntrials=rep(1,n))

summary(result1)

Y(i,j) ~Bin(Ntrial, p(i,j))

logit(p_rand(j)) ~Norm(0,sigma_j)

Any help is much appreciated,

Many thanks,

Isobel

The McFadden's pseudo-R squared, can be computed manually, using two
runs, like

> n = 10; y = rnorm(n); x = rnorm(n); r = inla(y ~ 1 + x, data =
data.frame(y,x), control.compute = list(dic=TRUE))
> r0 = inla(y ~ 1, data = data.frame(y,x), control.compute =
list(dic=TRUE))
> r$dic$deviance.mean
[1] 27.16944354
> r0$dic$deviance.mean
[1] 29.15843203
> 1 - r$dic$deviance.mean/r0$dic$deviance.mean
[1] 0.06821314949

or if you want to use the 'mean deviance' instead, its there is the dic
object.

H

When analyzing the inference results, I normally use inla.spde2.result to extract the marginal posterior of these parameters for a SPDE object. Is there any equivalent way of doing so but for the samples I obtain using inla.hyperpar.sample?

Thanks
-I

messages.body_plain:
I just posted a reply, but it doesn't seem to have gone through.  Anyway, the short answer is that I don't think the tie issue isn't relevant here.  The discussion of ties is specific to the use of partial likelihood to estimate the semi-parametric Cox model, no?  The survival models included as part of INLA are all parametric.  The coxph model uses a piecewise hazard function, with the relationship between periods characterized by a random walk.  The tell-tale sign that this is not the usual semi-parametric model is the presence of an intercept.  The piecewise random walk is, of course, extremely flexible, thus avoiding the problems that may come with stronger parametric assumptions.  In short, its in the same spirit as the semi-parmetric Cox model, but is not exactly equivalent.

Adam

messages.subject: Difference between multivariate correlated random effect model in INLA or in SAS
messages.subject_clean: Difference between multivariate correlated random effect model in INLA or in SAS
messages.body_plain:
Dear,

I am trying to fit a model for two responses. Each individual has a value for each of the two responses.
I want to model them by a covariate week, but want to allow a different effect for each response.

Doing this model in the following way in INLA:
result.indep.week.2resp<-inla(Y ~intercept1+intercept2+
weekenddummy1+weekenddummy2-1,
family=c("poisson","poisson"),data=first.full.2resp,
E=sumw,control.fixed=list(expand.factor.strategy='model.matrix'))

gives me the same results as modelling this using SAS.

However, when I want to include random effects, for each response 1 random effect and they might be correlated, the results are not alike anymore.
I can imagine some deviations, but now the precision and rho would indicate no correlation in INLA, whereas my estimates from SAS indicate a correlation.

The model I implemented in INLA is:
first.full.2resp$ID1<-rep(NA,dim(first.full.2resp)[1])
first.full.2resp$ID1[seq(1,n,2)]<-first.full.2resp$ID[seq(1,n,2)]
first.full.2resp$ID2<-rep(NA,dim(first.full.2resp)[1])
first.full.2resp$ID2[seq(2,n,2)]<-first.full.2resp$ID[seq(2,n,2)]
n.id <http://n.id><-length(unique(first.full.2resp$ID))

first.full.2resp$IDsort<-sort(rep(seq(1:n.id <http://n.id>),2))

result.dep.week.2resp.simplifiedLP<-inla(Y ~intercept1+intercept2+
weekenddummy1+weekenddummy2-1+f(IDsort,model="iid2d",n=2*n.id <http://n.id>,
hyper=list(theta=list(param=c(4,1.1380,0.3430,-0.4029)))),
family=c("poisson","poisson"),data=first.full.2resp,
E=sumw,control.fixed=list(expand.factor.strategy='model.matrix'),
control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace"))

(No difference between the strategies in control.inla.) The hyperparameter values are based on my variance and covariance estimates from SAS: (var1=0.8787, var2=2.9153 and covar=-0.6449).

Am I misinterpreting the precision to be exactly the precision and the same for the rho estimates?
Or is there something in the model that I am overseeing?

Kind regards,
Kim

control.mode=list(restart=T, theta=c(4,1,-1))

where the theta vector is the internal hyper-parameters.

Regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.subject: Error fitting zero-zero data using a zero inflated Poisson model
messages.subject_clean: Error fitting zero-zero data using a zero inflated Poisson model
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am modelling point process data with INLA and have successfully been using family="poisson" in the inla call to fit my data, along the lines of Ch 13 and 14 of the SPDE tutorial.

Now I would like to expand the standard Poisson model to a zero inflated Poisson model. However, using family="zeroinflatedpoissonX" with either of X=0,1,2 gives the error:

*** ERROR ***  INLA.Data1: Poisson like data[0] (y,e) = (0,0) is void

I believe this is related to the fact that I have some occurrences with no observations (y=0), which are given zero weight (e=0) in my data. With family="poisson" this is handled nicely (simply setting the likelihood contribution to zero, I believe).

Shouldn't the zero inflated model behave in the same way? Or is there a reason why 0-0 is not supported with the zero inflated models?

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Error fitting zero-zero data using a zero inflated Poisson model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Error fitting zero-zero data using a zero inflated Poisson model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,
I'm not sure a zero-inflated poison makes sense in that context. If you're trying to model detection probabilities, it comes out differently.

With known probabilities it's in our point processes with SPDEs paper, for unknown detection probability, you need to make use of strong information about the measurement protocol. A good example is this paper https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.06013

Best wishes,

Dan

Sent from my iPad

messages.subject: Can INLA be used to model 3D Cartesian data?
messages.subject_clean: Can INLA be used to model 3D Cartesian data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, all

I am wondering whether INLA can be applied to model y=f(x)+\epsilon, x \in R^3, \epsilon is Gaussian noise?

In INLA, \alpha=2 by default, and 0=<\alpha<2 is also possible.  Since \alpha=\nu+d/2 and d=3 in our case, I am not sure whether \nu=1/2 can properly model the data correlation.

On the other hand , does "2" in "inla.spde2.matern" in INLA means only x \in R^2 can be modeled, not for 3D data?

Looking forward to your reply!

Kindly Regards
Liye

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can INLA be used to model 3D Cartesian data?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can INLA be used to model 3D Cartesian data?
messages.body_plain:
It's possible, yes, but we don't have a simple interface for 3D spde domains yet.
For now, you'd have to construct the sparse finite element matrices for your 3D domain yourself, and call inla.spde2.generic() to construct the model object. How easy or hard that would be depends on your domain. I'm currently working on some updates for the mesh & spde models, so there may soon be some basic support for this built into the package.  What kind of domain and discretisation are you interested in?  A tetrahedralized domain, or a 3D lattice?

Finn
